headline: How to Remove Black Scorch Marks from an Iron Soleplate
snippet: Black scorch marks on an iron's soleplate can ruin clothing during the first pass. If the appliance leaves dark streaks or catches on fabric, the surface can often be restored using common household items rather than replacing the unit. Coarse salt is effective for removing burned fabric particles and mineral buildup from metal surfaces. To apply this method, spread a thin, even layer of fine table salt on a sheet of heavy paper or foil. Heat the iron to a medium temperature with the steam function turned off. Drag the hot soleplate across the salt crystals until the debris lifts away. Once the iron cools, wipe the surface with a dry, soft cloth. This abrasive approach is strictly for bare metal bases, such as stainless steel or aluminum. Salt must not be used on non-stick coatings like Teflon or ceramic, as the grains will scratch the surface and permanently damage the finish. For coated plates, a dedicated cleaning pencil is the safer option.

headline: The NHS accidentally bought the most valuable AI capability in enterprise software
snippet: The NHS could already have access to one of the most significant developments in enterprise artificial intelligence, but the technology is barely being used. On 3 August, Palantir reported quarterly revenue of $1.94bn, up 93% on the previous year. US commercial revenue grew 149%. The company closed $3.37bn in new contract value in a single quarter, and its market capitalisation now sits at roughly $440bn, making it one of the thirty most valuable companies on the planet. Citi upgraded the stock to “Buy”. Wedbush sees a path to a trillion-dollar valuation within three years. The CEO described the results as "otherworldly" and told CNBC the growth would continue for at least another eighteen months. The question every investor is trying to answer is what justifies that number. Revenue is growing fast, but not fast enough on its own to explain a valuation at 150 times trailing earnings. The answer Wall Street has settled on is a specific capability: a way of organising data that turns artificial intelligence from a promising experiment into an operational tool that can reason about an organisation the way a human operator would. The NHS Federated Data Platform (FDP), built on Palantir's Foundry, is live across 139 trusts with tens of thousands of users running national products for waiting list management, discharge planning and theatre scheduling. That is not what this article is about. This article is about the layer above those products: the AI capability that sits on top of the ontology, which Wall Street is pricing as the most valuable development in enterprise software, and which the NHS has deployed to a dozen or so individuals across a handful of trusts. What the ontology is, and what it does for AI Every large organisation has data spread across dozens of systems. Hospitals have electronic patient record systems (EPRs), patient administration systems, rostering platforms, bed management tools, pharmacy systems, test result repositories, and dozens more. The traditional approach to making this data useful is to extract it into a warehouse and write queries against it. That works for reporting. It does not work well for artificial intelligence (AI), because a warehouse knows about tables and columns but does not know what a patient is, what an admission means, how a referral relates to a pathway, or what discharge means operationally. An ontology is a structured model of how an organisation actually works. It defines the objects that exist in the business (patients, clinicians, wards, appointments, equipment, medications), the relationships between them (a patient is treated at a hospital, by a clinician, using equipment, following a pathway), and the actions that can be taken on them (discharge, refer, escalate, book). When an AI model runs against an ontology rather than against a flat data warehouse, it is not guessing at patterns in tables. It is reasoning about the organisation the way a human operator would, because the model of the organisation has been made explicit. This is what Palantir built into Foundry, the platform underneath FDP. It is not a database or a semantic layer sitting on top of one. It is an operational model of the business that AI can navigate, query, and act on. Foundry also provides the AI models themselves: multiple large language models including Claude, GPT, Gemini and others, hosted inside the platform, maintained and updated by Palantir. What the NHS procured and what the NHS ended up sitting on are two different things. Tom Bartlett A trust does not need to separately procure, deploy, host, or govern any of them. The models and the ontology arrive together, governed together, inside the same data boundary. That combination is where the value sits. Access to AI models is becoming commonplace; any organisation can call an API. What almost nobody has is the ontology that gives those models the operational context to produce answers worth acting on. Morgan Stanley concluded in March 2026 that Palantir's ontology is likely to remain a competitive advantage because replicating it would take years, and no competitor currently offers the combination at production scale. The evidence Wall Street is pricing The longest-running example is Airbus. The partnership began in 2015 and produced the Skywise platform, which maps every aircraft, every component, every sensor reading, every maintenance event, and every supply chain node into a single ontology. Over 100 airlines are on the platform, with 50,000 daily users. One carrier avoided 35 technical cancellations in a single month through predictive maintenance models running on the ontology. Another saved $13m in fuel costs. In April 2026, Airbus merged Skywise into a 750-person subsidiary and projected the platform could unlock $83bn in annual operational savings by 2044. But Airbus is a decade ahead. The more telling comparison is the cohort that started at roughly the same time as the NHS. In mid-2023, around the same period the FDP contract was signed, Palantir launched intensive AI workshops where companies bring their own data and build a working AI application in one to five days, specifically targeting AI use cases running on the ontology. By the end of 2023, over 500 had been completed across 465 organisations. By mid-2024, over 1,300. By 2025, the pace had reached nearly six per day. The commercial results from that cohort drove US commercial revenue from roughly $150 million per quarter in early 2023 to $764 million in the second quarter of 2026. These are not technology startups. Lear Corporation, a $20 billion automotive parts manufacturer, expanded across manufacturing, procurement and finance and reported significant cost savings. GE Aerospace, SAP, and Centrus Energy all presented at Palantir's customer conference in March 2026, showing what they had built on the same platform in two years. Tampa General Hospital built a sepsis detection tool on the same ontology pattern, identifying high-risk patients and tracking time-sensitive interventions through a clinical interface. The same company, the same technology, the same ontology architecture, launched in the same window as FDP. What the NHS has, and how it got here by accident When NHS England published the FDP tender in 2022 and 2023, it was procuring a data platform. The specification covered data integration, operational products, and analytical capability. The target architecture document listed AI and machine learning under "Future Directions," alongside event-driven architecture and the single patient record. There was no mention of ontology-grounded AI reasoning, no mention of hosted large language models, and no mention of anything resembling what Palantir would ship six months later. Palantir launched its AI platform in April 2023. The FDP contract was signed in November 2023. What the NHS procured and what the NHS ended up sitting on are two different things. The FDP now provides access to those models, all running inside the trust's own data boundary. Patient data does not leave the building. It is not sent to a data centre in Virginia to train a model. It is not handed to a frontier AI lab whose business model depends on absorbing its customers' proprietary data. Palantir CEO Alex Karp's argument, made forcefully after the Q2 results, is that enterprises using frontier AI through external APIs are paying to give away their competitive advantage, their "alpha." In Palantir's framing, an organisation's data is its treasure, and the richness of that data is where the alpha lives. The ontology keeps the data, the logic, the actions, and the security inside the customer's own boundary. For the NHS, that means patient data stays inside the trust, governed by the trust, with no training data leaving the perimeter. Palantir calls this the walled garden, and it is the answer to the question every Caldicott guardian in the country is asking about AI. Almost nobody has connected FDP to the answer. So what does this look like in practice? A capability called AskFDP allows clinical and operational staff to query their trust's data in natural language, with the AI reasoning against the ontology rather than running blind against a warehouse. The capability is live, it works, and it has been shaped by direct feedback from the trusts testing it, with substantial improvements over recent months. This has the potential to transform the use of data for reporting and decision-making across the NHS. Currently the capacity of any trust to turn its data into insight is constrained by the size and skills of its data team. With AskFDP, that constraint begins to dissolve. Operational managers and clinicians can interrogate their own data without waiting for an analyst to write a query, and data teams can redirect their effort toward the harder problems that still need human judgement. Yet it is being used by a dozen or so individuals across a handful of trusts. We find ourselves in an incredibly serendipitous situation. The NHS procured a data platform to a 2022 specification and ended up with a capability that the rest of the world is racing to deploy. The question is whether the NHS recognises that, or whether it continues to evaluate FDP against a specification that the technology has already outgrown. Why the NHS is falling behind on its own platform The private sector organisations that started on this technology in 2023 had a reason to move fast and nobody trying to stop them. When Lear Corporation ran its first workshop, the chief executive wanted competitive advantage and sent people with the authority to commit. When the workshop produced a working application in three days, there was no six-month governance review, no campaign group, and no select committee recommending the contract be cancelled. The NHS had none of those conditions. Start with how the programme was presented to trusts. NHS England's Medium Term Planning Framework tells every trust to onboard to FDP by 2028/29 and use its core products for elective recovery, cancer and urgent and emergency care. Trusts are told to use FDP for data warehousing and to implement the canonical data model. That presents FDP as a set of applications someone else has built for you, and a replacement for a data warehouse you already have in technology your staff already know. The AI capability is not mentioned anywhere in the guidance. In a federated architecture, each trust owns its instance and has a responsibility to understand what tools it has access to and develop a strategy for maximising them. The centre's job is to communicate what is available. Neither side is doing its part. The guidance told trusts to adopt someone else's apps and replace a warehouse, when the opportunity is to build their own applications and get ahead with AI. Because the opportunity was never articulated, most trusts never invested in the capability to pursue it. AskFDP requires the Health Decision Suite, a warehouse layer that is free but demands skills in Foundry and NHS data domain knowledge that barely exist in the same person in the labour market. The trusts furthest forward have assembled this capability at their own cost, without a national funding line. The handful of trusts that have reached the AI layer are now putting AskFDP through their own governance processes individually, answering the same questions in isolation, which is precisely the kind of duplication FDP was supposed to eliminate. The politics are important here. trusts know that publicly adopting anything built on Palantir's platform carries a risk of appearing in the next campaign briefing or parliamentary question, and that the rolling contract structure offers no certainty even to those willing to take that risk. Extension decisions in 2027 and at intervals thereafter mean the question of whether FDP survives is never settled for long enough to invest against. The NHS signed a seven-year contract and has spent two of those years debating whether to honour it, and a trust board looking at that pattern has every reason to conclude that waiting is safer than building. The deployment model that broke through equivalent caution in the private sector, intensive workshops on the customer's site producing a working AI application within a week, was attempted in the NHS as broader hackathons for those with the capacity and backing to attend. That self-selects for the trusts already furthest forward and leaves out the ones that would benefit most. The £10bn blind spot In July 2026, NHS England announced a major AI rollout backed by £10 bn of government funding over three years, supporting the 10 Year Health Plan's ambition to make the NHS "the most AI-enabled care system in the world." The programme covers AI triage via the NHS App, ambient voice technology for clinical notetaking, and the AI Algorithmic Improvement Programme. It barely mentions the FDP. It does not mention the ontology, AskFDP, the walled garden, or the governed AI capability already deployed across 139 trusts. The NHS AI strategy and the NHS data platform strategy exist as parallel workstreams, and the connection between them has been drawn only in the narrowest terms. Why has this connection not been made? The people closest to the FDP programme understand the AI potential of the platform they built. AskFDP was commissioned deliberately. Yet the institutional silence around FDP, driven by political sensitivity about the supplier and the contract review, appears to have prevented that understanding from reaching the policy documents that connect it to the national AI ambition. The 10 Year Health Plan does not mention FDP. The Medium Term Planning Framework treats it as elective recovery infrastructure. The AI strategy does not reference it as governed AI infrastructure. The culture of silence has not just prevented Trusts from adopting. It has prevented the NHS from connecting its own AI strategy to the platform best positioned to deliver it. The government is spending £10bn to make the NHS the most AI-enabled care system in the world. It already has governed AI running inside trust data boundaries on a platform deployed across 139 organisations, with an ontology that gives AI the operational context to produce answers clinicians can act on. The £10bn programme as announced is focused on the NHS App and ambient notetaking. The FDP programme has built an AI capability that appears in none of the published strategy documents. Whether by design or by the gravitational pull of political caution, these two programmes do not appear to be talking to each other. NHS England may well have a clear view of where this is heading. But the AI capability on FDP will not succeed as a centrally built and centrally delivered programme alone. It will succeed when trusts are building their own AI applications on the platform, when health technology companies are integrating with the ontology through the Solution Exchange, and when the frontline understands what it has access to and is equipped to use it. There are data engineers, analysts, clinicians and health technology founders across this country who would be energised by what is now possible on FDP, if they knew it was there. The capability is within their grasp. Someone needs to tell them. headline: Assam Police seize yaba tablets worth Rs 60 lakh, arrest two
snippet: Digital Desk | Guwahati, Oct 2 (IANS) Assam Police have seized a large consignment of suspected narcotic tablets worth around Rs 60 lakh and arrested two persons in Hailakandi district, officials said on Friday. The operation was carried out as part of intensified action against the trafficking and illegal transportation of narcotic substances in the district. According to officials, police recovered 816.9 grams of suspected Yaba tablets during the operation. Two persons, identified as Baharul Alam Majumdar and Chayekh Hussain Laskar, were arrested in connection with the seizure. Officials said the accused were taken into custody after police intercepted them and recovered the contraband from their possession. The seized tablets are suspected to be Yaba, a synthetic drug containing methamphetamine and caffeine and commonly trafficked across the northeastern region. The estimated street value of the seized contraband is around Rs 60 lakh, officials said. A case has been registered, and further investigation is underway to establish the source of the drugs and identify the intended recipients. Investigators are also examining whether the arrested persons are linked to a larger inter-state narcotics trafficking network operating through Assam and neighbouring states. Police are questioning the two accused to gather information about the supply chain, including the origin of the consignment, its intended destination and other persons allegedly involved in the network. The latest seizure comes amid stepped-up operations by law enforcement agencies in Assam against the trafficking of synthetic drugs and other narcotic substances. Officials said surveillance and checking have been intensified in vulnerable areas and along routes suspected to be used for transporting narcotics. The police are also examining the financial trail associated with the seized consignment and other evidence gathered during the operation. Further details are expected as the investigation progresses. The seizure of the suspected Yaba tablets is being viewed as a significant breakthrough in the ongoing crackdown on narcotics trafficking in Hailakandi and adjoining areas. Police said strict legal action would be taken against those found involved in the trafficking or distribution of the banned substances.

headline: REMAIN First Reactions Tease a “Heartbreaking” and "Scary as Hell" M. Night Shyamalan Thriller
snippet: M. Night Shyamalan just gave Beyond Fest audiences an unexpected early look at his next supernatural thriller, and it sounds like Remain might hit viewers right in the heart before scaring the hell out of them. M. Night Shyamalan, the filmmaker behind The Sixth Sense , Unbreakable , Signs , and Split , surprised fans with an impromptu screening of Remain at the 2026 Beyond Fest, and the first reactions coming out of the premiere have been overwhelmingly positive. Considering how wildly audiences can disagree over a Shyamalan movie, that's certainly encouraging. His films tend to spark plenty of debate once the credits roll, with The Sixth Sense and perhaps Unbreakable standing among his most universally embraced work. Remain stars Jake Gyllenhaal as Tate Gordon, a reclusive architect who moves to a small coastal town to finish his latest project. His life takes an unexpected turn when he meets an alluring young woman played by Phoebe Dynevor , who draws him out of isolation and into something far more dangerous. The recent trailer initially plays like a romantic drama about two strangers falling for each other, but this is a Shyamalan movie, so romance isn't the only thing waiting for Tate. It certainly appears that Dynevor's mysterious character may be a ghost, although there's a good chance the movie has a few more cards to play before revealing exactly what's happening. The unusual mix of romance and supernatural suspense comes from a collaboration between Shyamalan and bestselling author Nicholas Sparks, whose books include The Notebook . Shyamalan recently explained how their partnership began: “My new movie began with a conversation, an unexpected one, with a celebrated author, Nicholas Sparks. He sold more than 130 million books worldwide and wrote one of the most iconic love stories ever, The Notebook. “Romance is his territory. Mine’s a little different. I’m drawn to suspense, to twists and tension and stories that leave you just a little unsettled long after they are over. That feels like home to me.” He continued: “We started from nothing, just a couple of questions: What scares you? What moves you? What stays with you? We challenged each other. We traded ideas and slowly wove two very different perspectives into a single, thrilling, supernatural love story. In the end, we get to tell it our own way. Mine through film, Nicholas through his novel.” This is a pretty fascinating pairing. Sparks knows his way around emotional romance, while Shyamalan loves taking seemingly ordinary situations and pulling them into increasingly strange territory. Judging by the early Beyond Fest response, that combination may have produced something both scary and heartbreaking. Warner Bros. Pictures describes the movie as an unprecedented collaboration between Sparks and Shyamalan, with the official synopsis reading: "When reclusive architect Tate Gordon moves to a small coastal town to complete his latest project, he encounters an alluring young woman who pulls him out of his shell, and into the center of a deadly mystery that hangs over the town." Gyllenhaal and Dynevor are joined by Ashley Walters , Julie Hagerty , and Jay O. Sanders . The first reactions coming out of Beyond Fest describe Remain as "scary as hell" and "heartbreaking," which is an intriguing combination for a supernatural love story. If Shyamalan and Sparks really managed to make the romance matter as much as the mystery, this could be one of the director's more interesting genre swings. headline: Wärtsilä, Schneider Electric and Stanley Consultants launch coordinated approach for faster U.S. data center power delivery
snippet: Coordinated "Generator-to-Chip" approach integrates onsite generation, electrical infrastructure and engineering to help data center customers streamline development and save time compared to traditional delivery models. HOUSTON , Oct. 1, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Technology group Wärtsilä, Schneider Electric and Stanley Consultants have developed an innovative "Generator-to-Chip" approach to help U.S. data center developers and operators bring scalable power capacity online faster. Designed around the AI load, the approach aligns onsite power generation, electrical infrastructure, automation, engineering and project execution from the outset. By connecting the power pathway from generation and electrical distribution to digital monitoring and the IT load, the approach reduces handoffs, improves coordination across critical interfaces and provides greater execution certainty. The combined approach can accelerate project schedules compared to traditional, sequential delivery models. From left to right: Melton Chang, Executive Vice President, Power Systems at Schneider Electric; Risto Paldanius, Vice President, Americas, Wärtsilä Energy; Tom Mergen, Vice President and Business Development Leader, Stanley Consultants Driven by accelerating investment in AI, demand for new data center capacity is growing rapidly across the United States. At the same time, lengthy grid interconnection timelines and delays in critical power infrastructure are slowing projects and increasing the need for coordinated solutions that can deliver dependable power where and when it is needed. Wärtsilä provides flexible, modular engine power plants that can deliver reliable onsite power generation, start rapidly and scale as data center demand grows. Schneider Electric contributes the integrated electrical architecture, automation and digital power management that coordinate power from generation to the AI load. Stanley Consultants provides technical and advisory services across the data center lifecycle, including engineering, permitting, design coordination, construction management, commissioning oversight and climate resilience expertise. "For many data center projects, power has become the schedule. Developers need reliable solutions that can be planned, built and delivered at the pace that AI growth demands. This innovative, integrated approach marks a significant step forward: by bringing our complementary capabilities together from the outset, we can simplify execution, reduce handoffs and shorten timelines. Most importantly, it gives customers a faster, clearer path from project planning to operational capacity," says Risto Paldanius, Vice President, Americas, Wärtsilä Energy. "AI growth is increasing the scale and speed required of data center power infrastructure," says Melton Chang, Executive Vice President, Power Systems at Schneider Electric. "An AI Energy Park starts with the load and coordinates generation, electrical infrastructure, automation and digital technologies as one system. This gives developers a scalable, grid-flexible path to bring high-density AI capacity online faster." "We are delighted to be part of a team that is focused on meeting our client's business outcomes and community needs," says Lance Sulzen, Vice President and Energy Market Leader at Stanley Consultants. "Integrated solutions help deliver functional, resilient, and scalable facilities effectively and efficiently. Taking a collaborative delivery approach helps us better identify risks, streamline interfaces and improve delivery confidence from concept to commissioning." Wärtsilä, Schneider Electric and Stanley Consultants collectively bring expertise in power generation, electrical distribution, digital control and project execution that is relevant to modern data center development. Together, these capabilities demonstrate how data center operators can address requirements for speed, reliability, scalability and operational flexibility across grid-connected, islanded and hybrid configurations. headline: India's office space absorption surges 8 pc to record 66.4 million sq ft in Jan–Sep: Report
snippet: New Delhi, Oct 1 (IANS) India's office sector recorded absorption of nearly 66.4 million sq. ft. in the January–September 2026 period, an 8 per cent increase year-on-year which is a record high for any nine-month period, a report said on Thursday. The report from CBRE South Asia said the total absorption during the July–September quarter (Q3) stood at nearly 21 million sq. ft., up 6 per cent on an annual basis. New supply during the period also reached nearly 51 million sq. ft., up 18 per cent YoY marking an all-time high for any nine-month period. Development completions in Q3 2026 totalled nearly 19 million sq. ft., up 26 per cent YoY, led by Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Pune. These three cities collectively accounted for nearly 89 per cent of quarterly completions, the report said. “Flex operators, BFSI and technology occupiers are all expanding simultaneously, while occupiers across the board continue to gravitate towards higher-quality buildings. That breadth of demand is what gives this cycle its durability," said Anshuman Magazine, Chairman and CEO, India, South-East Asia, Middle East and Africa, CBRE. Global Capability Centres leased nearly 8.7 million sq. ft. during the quarter, taking nine-month GCC absorption to a record 28 million sq. ft. accounting for 42 per cent of overall leasing. GCC space take-up volumes rose 16 per cent YoY over the nine months, and quarterly take-up was led by Hyderabad accounting for 37 per cent share and Bengaluru (28 per cent), the report noted. Within BFSI, GCCs accounted for a 76 per cent share of leasing during the quarter. "Three-fourths of the space taken up this quarter was in buildings under ten years old, and flex has become the largest demand driver. The core plus flex model has moved from an experiment to a strategic portfolio decision," said Ram Chandnani, Managing Director, Leasing Services, CBRE India. Over half of the new supply added in Q3 and 9M 2026 came from premium Grade A+ assets, the report noted. India's office sector is firmly positioned for another strong year as the momentum is underpinned by healthy occupier enquiries and subsequent deal closures as global and domestic enterprises continue to expand their portfolios, the report forecasted. Nearly 77 per cent of occupiers expect to expand their India office portfolios over the next two years. Steady economic growth and the country’s deep talent base are expected to sustain occupier activity despite a cautious global macroeconomic backdrop, reinforcing its appeal for corporate expansion. —IANS aar/ag

headline: Calm, disciplined and humble: Capt Smit Machchhar’s friends, neighbours in India recall heroic pilot's traits
snippet: Mumbai, Oct 1 (IANS) As Captain Smit Machchhar recovers from injuries sustained while helping avert a major mid-air crisis aboard a flydubai flight, friends and neighbours at his Mumbai residence have rallied around the pilot, recalling him as a calm, disciplined and humble person, who had grown up among them. Smit Machchhar, an Indian pilot with flydubai, was injured during a confrontation with the co-pilot aboard Flight FZ1073, which was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday. Despite his injuries, he managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to intervene. The aircraft was subsequently diverted and landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, with all 174 people on board reported safe. Back in Mumbai, those who watched Smit Machchhar grow up said his actions were consistent with the temperament they had known since childhood. Prateek Gandhi, a childhood friend and neighbour, told IANS that he felt proud seeing someone from his own building play such a crucial role in saving lives. “He was someone who grew up with us, and it makes me proud that someone from our building has contributed to such a cause,” Gandhi said. Recalling Smit Machchhar's composure, Gandhi said, “With his sixth sense and presence of mind, he saved 174 people.” He described Smit Machchhar as calm and composed since childhood and said those qualities may have helped him remain steady when the situation inside the aircraft turned critical. “A person might change, but the base of that person remains the same,” Gandhi said, adding that Smit Machchhar's calm demeanour could explain why he was able to respond to the crisis despite the circumstances. “Videos from inside the aircraft that have emerged since the incident also appeared to show Machchhar remaining composed,” he said. An older neighbour who has known Smit Machchhar's family for long, recalled seeing him play around the residential building as a child. “He used to play around in the building. While growing up, he kept to himself and never bothered anyone,” the neighbour said. He described Machchhar as disciplined and hardworking, qualities he believed helped him pursue an aviation career. “He was very disciplined and worked hard. That is how he became a pilot,” he said. Recalling the events that took place on the flight, the neighbour said he found it difficult to put his feelings into words. “I don't have words to explain how I felt after the incident,” he said. Another family friend described Machchhar as a humble and “amazing” person and told IANS she was praying for his safety and recovery. “He is a really good friend of mine. I am praying for his safety and hoping that he is doing well,” she said. She said Smit Machchhar's parents live in India, while his wife and children are based in Dubai. “He is wonderful and an amazing person, and just very humble,” she said. The family friend said Smit Machchhar's actions were particularly remarkable given that he himself was severely injured during the incident. Smit Machchhar, who previously spent more than 11 years with SpiceJet before joining flydubai in 2022, has more than 13 years of commercial flying experience.
